title: The Man Who Saw Cats in Human Faces

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student visits a campus neurologist to discuss unusual visual symptoms after a minor head injury.

script.en: Dr. Patel, thanks for seeing me on such short notice. I’m a second-year grad student in cognitive science, and I’ve been having these strange visual experiences for about three weeks now.
Of course. Tell me more about what you’ve been noticing. Are these experiences constant, or do they come and go?

They come and go. After I look at something for a while—say, a pattern on a computer screen or a poster on the wall—the image seems to linger even after I look away. It’s like a ghost image floating over whatever I look at next.
That sounds like palinopsia, where a visual image persists after the stimulus is removed. Have you had any head trauma recently?
I did fall off my bike about a month ago and hit my head. I didn’t lose consciousness, but I had a bad headache for a couple of days.

That could be relevant. Palinopsia can sometimes occur after minor head injuries, though it’s rare. Have you noticed any other distortions—like faces looking strange or objects appearing larger or smaller than they are?
Actually, yes. Sometimes when I’m in a crowd, people’s faces seem slightly distorted—like their eyes are too far apart or their mouths are twisted. It’s subtle, but it’s unsettling.

That’s an important detail. There’s a condition called prosopometamorphopsia, where faces appear distorted. It can co-occur with palinopsia, especially when the temporal lobe is involved. I’d like to refer you for an MRI to rule out any structural issues.
Is this something that could be permanent? I’m worried it might affect my research—I spend hours looking at faces in my experiments.

In many cases, these symptoms improve over time, particularly if there’s no underlying lesion. But we need to monitor you closely. In the meantime, try to reduce visual fatigue and avoid prolonged staring at high-contrast patterns.
I’ll do that. Should I keep a diary of when these episodes happen?
Yes, that would be very helpful. Note the time, what you were looking at, and how long the afterimage lasted. That will give us a clearer picture of what’s going on.

script.en: When we think of visual perception, we often assume that what we see is a direct reflection of the world around us. But research in cognitive neuroscience reveals that perception is far more constructive than we imagine. Our brains actively interpret sensory input, filling in gaps and making predictions based on past experience. Occasionally, this constructive process goes awry, producing striking perceptual distortions. One such phenomenon is palinopsia, in which an image persists in the visual field after the original stimulus has disappeared. Patients describe seeing a ghostly afterimage that lingers for seconds or even minutes, overlaying whatever they look at next. This condition is relatively rare and often associated with damage to the posterior visual pathways, particularly in the temporal or parietal lobes. While it can be distressing, many patients learn to adapt to these persistent images over time. Another unusual condition is prosopometamorphopsia, a disorder in which faces appear distorted. Patients may see features stretched, compressed, or displaced. In some cases, the distortion is so severe that familiar faces become unrecognizable. Like palinopsia, prosopometamorphopsia is linked to abnormalities in the temporal lobe, especially the fusiform gyrus, a region critical for face processing. Interestingly, some patients report that the distortions affect only human faces, leaving objects and animals unaffected, which supports the idea that the brain has specialized mechanisms for face perception. These conditions, though rare, offer valuable insights into how the brain constructs our visual world. They remind us that perception is not a passive recording but an active, dynamic process—one that can break down in fascinating and sometimes unsettling ways. For researchers, such cases provide a window into the neural architecture of vision, helping to map the complex pathways that allow us to recognize faces and navigate our environment.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The causes and treatments of common visual impairments.
How the brain constructs perception and what happens when it fails.
The role of the fusiform gyrus in recognizing familiar faces.

questions.explain: 文章首段提出感知是建构性的，随后介绍两种感知扭曲现象及其神经机制，末段总结这些现象揭示大脑如何建构视觉世界，B 正确。A 项偷换概念，文章聚焦罕见扭曲而非常见视觉损伤；C 项以偏概全，只是其中一个细节；D 项无中生有，未讨论恢复速度。
questions.evidence: These conditions, though rare, offer valuable insights into how the brain constructs our visual world.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is a characteristic of palinopsia?
options: It causes faces to appear distorted and unrecognizable.
It results from damage to the fusiform gyrus exclusively.
It makes an image persist after the stimulus is removed.
It affects only objects and not human faces.

questions.evidence: One such phenomenon is palinopsia, in which an image persists in the visual field after the original stimulus has disappeared.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the fusiform gyrus from the passage?
options: It is responsible for all types of visual perception.
It is more active when looking at objects than at faces.
It plays a specialized role in processing human faces.
It is the only brain region linked to face distortions.
questions.explain: 文中说 fusiform gyrus 是“a region critical for face processing”，且某些患者只有人脸受影响，说明该区域对人脸有专门作用，C 正确。A 项绝对化，原文只说对脸加工关键；B 项与原文相反；D 项绝对化，原文只说 especially，未说唯一。

sections.title: When Faces Turn into Cats: A Rare Visual Disorder
sections.passage:
Imagine seeing feline features superimposed on every human face you encounter throughout the day. For most people, this sounds like a scene from a fantasy novel. Yet for a 28-year-old man named Karl, it is a daily reality. Karl sees the eyes and stripes of his pet cat, Luna, flickering over the faces of people he meets, both in person and online. His experience offers a rare window into how the brain processes faces and what happens when those processes go awry.

Karl’s unusual visions began after surgery to remove abnormally connected blood vessels from his right posterior temporal lobe, a region critical for recognizing identity and reading facial expressions. Since the operation two years ago, he has experienced a combination of two rare neurological conditions: palinopsia, in which an image persists in the visual field after the stimulus is removed, and prosopometamorphopsia, in which faces appear distorted. In Karl’s case, the distortion takes an atypical form—face substitution, where one face is replaced by another.

The substitution works both ways. If Karl sees Luna first thing in the morning, her eyes and silver stripes appear on every human face he later encounters. Conversely, if the first face he sees is human, that person’s pupils and eye shape are superimposed on every other face, including Luna’s. These superimpositions are seamless: the faces otherwise appear normal and coherent. “Karl finds the transfers between cat and human faces very strange,” writes Brad Duchaine, a psychologist at Dartmouth University who has studied prosopometamorphopsia for years. “He has had problems with face perception for some time, though, so he has adapted to them and takes them in stride.”

Face substitution is an unusual expression of prosopometamorphopsia. Ordinarily, people with this condition see alterations in the shape or position of facial features or in the color or texture of skin. Some see eyes and mouths stretched into “demonic” shapes, or features drooping, swelling, or twisting. One of the earliest documented cases of face substitution, published in Cortex in 1986, involved a woman who, about nine months after a stroke, saw a poodle’s face on fellow bus passengers for about 30 minutes. At the time, the case suggested that the brain processes faces differently from other visual stimuli—an idea now widely accepted.

The cases of Karl and the 1986 patient differ in at least two ways. First, the woman saw the poodle’s whole face on passengers, whereas Karl sees only parts carried over, mainly the eyes and pupils. Second, the 1986 transfer went one way, from dog to human; Karl’s goes both ways. These distinctions highlight the variability of prosopometamorphopsia and the importance of studying individual cases. For researchers, such cases provide valuable clues about the neural architecture of face perception, helping to map the complex pathways that allow us to recognize faces and navigate our social world.

A rare face-substitution condition and its research value.
The historical development of face-perception studies.
The link between pet ownership and visual hallucinations.

options: A stroke that damaged his fusiform gyrus.

questions.stem: How does Karl’s case differ from the 1986 patient’s?

Karl’s substitution works both ways, while the woman’s was one-way.

options: He doubts that Karl’s case is scientifically valuable.
He believes Karl has adjusted to his perceptual problems.
He is convinced that Karl’s surgery was unnecessary.
He suspects that Karl is exaggerating his symptoms.

questions.stem: The word “seamless” in the third paragraph is closest in meaning to ______.
options: free from visible interruption
extremely colorful
temporary and unstable
difficult to perceive
questions.explain: “seamless”意为无缝的、连贯的，后文“正常且连贯”也提示叠加没有明显痕迹，A 项正确。B 项望文生义，与“无缝”无关；C 项与“正常连贯”矛盾；D 项偷换概念，无缝不等于难以察觉。
questions.evidence: These superimpositions are seamless: the faces otherwise appear normal and coherent.

long_sentences.en: The reverse is also true: If the first face he sees in the morning is a human one, he will see that person’s pupils and eye shape superimposed on every other face he sees that day, including the furry mug of his pet cat.
According to a case study published in Cortex in 1986, a woman known as “patient 2” was riding a bus about 9 months after a stroke when she saw a poodle in the lap of another passenger.
When Karl wakes in the morning, his gray tabby Luna is often the first being he greets, and Luna’s face, the first he gazes upon: the whiskers, the almond eyes, the pink nose, the stripes.
